M/S Drotten is the best ship because somebody put 50,400 kW of machinery inside a 196-metre passenger ferry and I apparently need an entire website to explain how much I love that. She does 28.5 knots. That’s about 52.8 km/h. Look at her SIZE and then think about that speed again.[1]

This is my Drotten site. The specification list is compulsory. scroll slowly.

The numbers [link]

Those figures come from Gotlandsbolaget’s fleet details. I keep the decimals because 25.67 is a perfectly good number and rounding it feels unnecessary.[2]

  • Built: 2003. Guangzhou Shipyard International, China
  • Ship type: Ro-ro passenger ferry. Passengers upstairs, vehicles rolling on and off the vehicle decks.
  • Length overall: 196 metres
  • Between perpendiculars: 176 metres. Different measurement, yes I want both.
  • Beam: 25.67 metres
  • Draught: 6.40 metres
  • Service speed: 28.5 knots. Approximately 52.8 km/h
  • Main machinery output: 50,400 kW. 50.4 MEGAWATTS.
  • Auxiliary machinery: Another 4,560 kW
  • Passenger capacity: 1,500 people
  • Vehicle capacity: 500 cars. Or 1,800 lane metres of cargo space
  • Gross tonnage: 29,746 GT. This measures internal volume; it isn’t the ship’s weight.
  • Deadweight: 5,174 tonnes
  • Ice class: 1A
  • IMO number: 9223796
  • Call sign: SGPI

Four. Wärtsilä. Engines. [link]

Engine type: Wärtsilä 46-series diesels. Wärtsilä supplied eight main engines across the two sister ships.[3]

Drotten’s exact engine listing: four Wärtsilä 12V46C engines. Four. I could have put this beside the power figure but then you might have scrolled past it.[4]

50,400 kW = 50.4 MEGAWATTS.
on a passenger ferry. I’m still not over this.

The Gotland name thing [link]

Drotten was M/S Gotland from 2003 to 2020, so finding an old photo with GOTLAND on her is like finding another bit of her photo album. I will open one picture to check the name and suddenly there are fourteen tabs and it’s late. Same ship, earlier name, years of crossings already behind her.

This is why I care about IMO 9223796 so much: names move around, and I want to know which actual hull I’m looking at. The 2003 Gotland became Drotten in 2020. I keep both names in my searches because otherwise you miss SEVENTEEN YEARS of her history.[4]
